d243d837c63c: Ask: “Ile metrów kwadratowych ma twój pokój? A ile metrów ma twój stół?”. Note 1–2 mistakes with the form — you will return to them on s3.
1aa6095cfb65: Quick round: you say the numbers 2, 12, 22, 21, 104, 111 — the learner immediately says them with «metr». The most common mistake is «dwadzieścia jeden metr».
e085f9961fa6: English does it the other way round: 2.5 metres — a point, not a comma, and a plural noun. Say it out loud, it is an easy win. In colloquial Polish you hear «2,5 metrów», but the norm is metra.
1d2e9aa8e6a9: The learner describes their own desk, door and window: one sentence for each construction. Make sure the genitive follows «ma»: długości, szerokości.
0db125ae399e: The main trap here: „two metres longer” → o dwa metry. Ask the student to compare two rooms in their flat in both ways.
ca5596d97bc5: Do not turn this into an “always/never” rule for everything: here are only the forms that will really come up in lessons. Półtorej is passive knowledge — recognising it is enough.
16f7e6247950: Write «12 : 3 = 4» on paper and ask the learner to read it in Polish. Most will say «dwanaście na trzy» — and that is exactly the topic.
165f1e2b3ca1: Learners confuse iloczyn / iloraz — hint: iloRaz as «raz po raz» (dividing again and again). The result words are needed for word problems with pairs.
0802770f62c2: Watch the dopełniacz (genitive) after z: «z dziewięciu», «z szesnastu» — the student will want to say «z dziewięć».
7cb75e283027: Litery czytamy po polsku: h to ha, nie „aitch”; V to fał, nie „vee”.
27d02ffaa348: The most common sticking point. Have the learner read 3–4 symbols from their own lecture notes.
420f92f40aae: The student reads each formula aloud twice: slowly, then at normal speed.
d15c6bb6f1c5: Ask the student to find one such task in their university notes and read it aloud.
d7d748ebb4cf: Say each trap in English first and let the student translate it themselves — only then reveal the correct version.
